To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the preconditioning effect on the linear least squares problem depends on the relative eigenstructure of the model and weight matrices; 2) in the context of weakly constrained 3D Var data assimilations, the model and weight matrix are not necessarily similar, so that the use of a preconditioner is not guaranteed to improve the convergence rate.

(i) a preconditioner that is based on an approximation of the Hessian of a weighted least squares problem can be very inefficient, (ii) this is due to the interplay of eigenstructures of the model and weighting matrix, (iii) this can be understood by the fact that the preconditioner is based on the inverse of the model matrix and not on the inverse of a weighted model matrix, (iv) in the case of weakly constrained 3D Var data assimilaton,

(i) the preconditioner should be chosen such that it is as close as possible to the weighting matrix, and (ii) the preconditioner must not be chosen such that the eigenstructure of the model and preconditioner is too similar.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of preconditioning a least squares problem using the model matrix, and the consequences in a data assimilation context.
the question: how does preconditioning the weighted linear least squares (WLLS) problem affect the solution of the weakly constraint 4D Var (WC 4D Var) problem?
the question: how can one best precondition weighted least squares problems?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in general, the use of a preconditioner for a weighted linear least squares problem is only justified if a priori information is available that allows the choice of the preconditioner to be based on this information.
, in the context of weakly constrained variatonal data assimilation, the use of the model matrix as preconditioner for the weighted least squares problem is not recommended.
the preconditioner should be chosen with great care.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of a preconditioner in the weakly constrained case is not as beneficial as it is in the strongly constrained case.
, for a given problem, the optimal preconditioner is problem specific and should be chosen accordingly.
the use of a preconditioner for the weighted linear least squares problem is only justified if the eigenvalue spectrum of the weighting matrix is well separated from that of the model matrix.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the case of weak constraints, a preconditioner should be used only if the weighting matrix has an eigenstructure that is very different from that of the model matrix.
the use of preconditioners for the linear weighted least square problem is not recommended in general.
the choice of preconditioners in the context of data assimilation problems should take the structure of the problem into account, and not only the structure of the linear model.
